For example, the pattern template for pattern-oriented software architecture includes a section that describes the problem addressed by the pattern [3]. In addition to capturing the essence of the design problem, this section documents the forces operating on the problem. These forces identify aspects of the problem that should be considered in the solution. They might be, for example, performance requirements, constraints about allowable protocols, or desirable properties of solutions. They may be in competition with each other, thereby forcing consideration of design tradeoffs. For example, forces for the pipe and filter architecture include the desirability of small processing steps, the expectation that non-adjacent filters do not share information, and the error-prone-ness of explicit storage of intermediate results by users (which motivates the use of pipes for communication).

Design obligations are design-level responsibilities that are analogous to proof obligations, good coding practices, integrity constraints, guidelines, and the like. For example, proving loop invariants in a programming language requires inductive proofs. Similarly, some architectures rely on specific relations among components that impose design obligations to establish and preserve these critical relations. For example, databases rely on integrity constraints, and event systems require the designer to ensure that the collection of event handlers will, in aggregate, properly field all the events that are raised. Hoare laid out the proof obligations for the representations of abstract data types [5]; this is the example of Section III. In feedback-based adaptive control, a set of obligations arise from the relations that must be assured among elements of the feedback process; this is the example of Section IV.

At all software levels, including code, architecture, design, and requirements, there are languages or language-like constructs that guide allowable design representations. These do not generally include all constraints that assure that the definitions will fully satisfy the expectations of the paradigm. The additional constraints, or expectations, are often tacit; they may sometimes be inferred from API documentation. Nevertheless, they create obligations on developers beyond the languages’ rules on what can be defined1. I’m interested here in design obligations , the additional expectations that shape whether designs that are well-formed in a language or paradigm will actually be satisfactory. These are obligations that arise from the domain of the design paradigm itself; they are not specifications or rationales for particular designs developed in the paradigm.

Accordingly, the design obligations should refer only to the design paradigm. Explanations of the rationale for specific design decisions in a particular implementation and specifications of application-specific policies, for example with session contracts, is also important—but it’s a different undertaking; the design obligations are one source of issues to address in those specifications.

Whenever designers decide to approach a problem by introducing an abstraction, they incur an obligation to establish consistency between the abstraction and the system it abstracts from (as discussed in section I.E). Hoare describes one important approach, giving the design obligations for the abstraction layer associated with abstract data types [5]. This technique applies as well to other abstractions, for example transform spaces, simulations, model-driven design, and higherlevel languages. Even in high-level design, there are primitives, constructs, and compositions; the designer needs to understand the additional responsibilities associated with satisfying the expectations.

Define an invariant for the representation. This is an integrity constraint: a predicate that says whether the values in the implementation represent a legal value. For example, a stack implemented as a vector and an index into the vector would have an invariant that limits the index to values within the vector. The commonlyused MAPE architecture for adaptive systems also does not call for designers to be explicit about how they actually achieve control [7]. It is valuable to make design obligations explicit—but what are these obligations here? We can identify some of them by looking carefully at the structure of feedback control to find obligations that apply also to higher-level adaptive control. For example, the designer of an adaptive system that is supposed to maintain some parameter at a reference value should show that the system is controllable (the reference value is achievable), stable (control actions do move the system to the reference value), and robust (it’s stable despite external disturbances).

A Dagstuhl on self-adaptive systems [4] explored in depth the application of control theory to self-adaptive systems. In particular, we identified the limitations of classical control theory for large-scale adaptive systems, showed how aspects of classical control could nonetheless guide design, and worked through several case studies [6]. These ideas are perhaps more accessible in a related video [13], which examines the components of a feedback loop and identifies design obligations—properties that the designer must address—as shown in the boxed annotations in Figure 2. They call out the need for the designer to consider  what are the important properties to control  how the reference level is determined  how well the tracked metric estimates the real process state, and what proxy might suffice if direct measurement isn’t possible  what operations on the process are available, and are they adequate for full control  how the corrections are determined, and what effect a correction has on the process  whether the available operations on the process are sufficient to maintain control  what external disturbances are possible, and whether it is possible to compensate for them with process inputs These are essential questions that the usual software development methods and tools, do not address.

It isn’t sufficient to write code or lay out a design in whatever notation is available. When designing within a framework, paradigm, or other norm, the designer often has additional obligations to ensure certain properties of the design. Unfortunately, these are often informal or implicit. This position paper calls out the need for more systematic, even more formal, recognition and documentation of these obligations. Doing so would benefit both the learning and the checking of these obligations.

title: Designing Dialogic Disclaimers: Principles for Ethical Conversational Design in LLM Interfaces
abstract: Current disclaimer approaches in large language model (LLM) systems often disrupt conversational flow with static, one-shot warnings that fail to engage users in deeper ethical reflection and, as a growing body of evidence reveals, are largely ineffective at achieving their intended goals of calibrated trust and informed use. This paper examines how disclaimers can be reimagined as integrated dialogic elements that maintain conversational coherence while effectively communicating necessary ethical information. Through a theoretical synthesis drawing on research in conversational repair, dialogue structure, AI transparency, and empirical studies of user interaction with LLMs, we identify four design principles for dialogic disclaimers: Conversational Continuity, Contextual Adaptation, Layered Communication, and User Agency. We provide illustrative conversation patterns demonstrating how these principles can transform disclaimers from disruptive and often ignored statements into constructive components of ethical dialogue. This work establishes a conceptual framework intended as a theoretical foundation to guide future empirical evaluation and the design of more ethically responsible and conversationally fluent LLM interfaces.

Our main contribution is a conceptual framework of four design principles for dialogic disclaimers: Conversational Continuity, Contextual Adaptation, Layered Communication, and User Agency. These aim to transform disclaimers into integral, effective components of ethical dialogue. We illustrate these with conversation patterns, acknowledging practical nuances and trade-offs. This work provides a theoretical foundation for future empirical evaluation and the design of more ethically responsible, conversationally fluent LLM interfaces.

Moreover, analyses of commercial LLM systems reveal inconsistent transparency practices, such as "riskcorrelated transparency" where disclosures vary by domain rather than by consistent principle [5]. This body of evidence collectively underscores a critical failure of current disclaimer strategies, demanding a shift towards more integrated and effective approaches.

LLM Contexts Traditional conversational theories require careful adaptation for LLM contexts due to the unique characteristics of LLMs, such as their asymmetric knowledge, statistical rather than belief-based understanding, and lack of genuine communicative intent. Interface designs that are overly anthropomorphic can lead to user misinterpretations of LLM capabilities. The observed inconsistencies in how current systems manage and disclose their knowledge boundaries and operational risks [5] further underscore the necessity for new, tailored frameworks for ethical communication in human-AI interaction.

We propose four principles, drawing on insights from several key areas: conversation analysis [12]; research on LLM communication challenges, including grounding gaps [ 13] and the need for AIspecific maxims [10]; the documented failures of static disclaimers [3, 4, 9, 11]; the problematic nature of LLM explanations [ 1, 15]; and calls for more actionable, human-centered XAI [2, 5, 8]. These principles aim to transform disclaimers into integrated dialogic

Disclaimers should maintain conversational flow and topical coherence. This principle addresses the "grounding gap" in LLMs [13] and their deviation from human conversational maxims [10], which can cause miscalibrated trust. Abrupt disclaimers risk user frustration [3] and are less likely to be processed than smoothly integrated ones [9], which align with the preference for self-repair in conversation [12] and the potential for better transparency in dialogue [5]. • Design implications: Integrate disclaimers using linguistic transitions and consistent tone, avoiding isolated statements that users ignore [ 11, 14] and working with, not against, human conversational expectations [4]. Disclaimers should explicitly link to the current topic and user query to reduce cognitive load and bridge grounding gaps.

Disclaimers should provide concise warnings in-flow, with detailed explanations accessible on request. This is crucial as LLM outputs can be plausible yet unfaithful [15], incomplete, or "adversarially helpful" [1], and LLMs may not signal knowledge boundaries [15] or maintain epistemic caution [ 5]. Layering respects user attention, prevents overload, and allows user-initiated access to critical details for calibrated trust. This aligns with diegetic/extradiegetic communication [2] and "seamful" design [7, 8]. • Design implications: Keep core disclaimers brief and relevant. Offer intuitive, low-friction ways for users to access details (e.g., explicit prompts, hyperlinks, interactive elements). This gives users control over information depth, helping them see beyond potentially misleading explanations [1, 15].

Our principles and patterns offer a conceptual basis for dialogic LLM disclaimers. This responds to the failure of static approaches, which often result in a ’lose-lose’ situation: minimal behavioral impact despite user confusion or miscalibrated confidence [3]. Users frequently ignore, forget, or misunderstand static warnings [4, 9, 14], sometimes preferring unmarked falsehoods [11]. Our dialogic approach seeks more salient, memorable, and effective ethical communication integrated into the conversation.

Adopting these principles requires LLMs with deeper dialogue awareness (given "grounding gaps" [ 13] and "uncertainty maintenance variance" [5]) and careful design for layered information and user engagement. Tensions exist: Agency can increase cognitive load; Adaptation may reduce predictability; Continuity might conflict with compliance needs. Disclaimer fatigue [ 1] is a risk, requiring strategies like risk-proportionate frequency. Since LLMs can generate unfaithful or adversarially helpful explanations [1, 15], dialogic disclaimers must also foster skepticism and equip users for verification.

This framework embodies ethical commitments: Continuity respects user cognition [9, 12]; Adaptation operationalizes proportionality [5]; Layered Communication supports informed consent regarding potentially misleading systems [2, 15]; User Agency challenges paternalism and promotes critical thinking [8, 11]. Navigating trade-offs (e.g., Transparency vs. Usability) requires contextual judgment. Our principles extend practical strategies like contextual disclosure and reflective checkpoints [5], offering a robust approach to these trade-offs.

This paper is theoretical; empirical validation is vital. The principles are a framework, not a universal solution, and may not suit all contexts (e.g., time-critical tasks). They address ethical communication, not underlying LLM biases, though informed by how systems communicate these issues [5] and the nature of LLM outputs [1, 15]. Effectiveness also depends on LLMs’ ability for nuanced self-dialogue about limitations [10, 13].

Designing Dialogic Disclaimers: Principles for Ethical Conversational Design in LLM Interfaces CUI ’25, July 08–10, 2025, Waterloo, ON, Canada These principles aim to smoothly integrate ethical considerations, adapt them to context, layer information to manage cognitive load and address issues like unfaithful LLM explanations [ 1, 15], and empower user reflection. While empirical validation is vital, this framework offers a foundation for designing more ethically sound and conversationally effective LLM interactions. Adopting a dialogic approach is a promising and urgently needed step.

title: Design principles for data analysis
abstract: The data science revolution has led to an increased interest in the practice of data analysis. While much has been written about statistical thinking, a complementary form of thinking that appears in the practice of data analysis is design thinking – the problem-solving process to understand the people for whom a product is being designed. For a given problem, there can be significant or subtle differences in how a data analyst (or producer of a data analysis) constructs, creates, or designs a data analysis, including differences in the choice of methods, tooling, and workflow. These choices can affect the data analysis products themselves and the experience of the consumer of the data analysis. Therefore, the role of a producer can be thought of as designing the data analysis with a set of design principles. Here, we introduce design principles for data analysis and describe how they can be mapped to data analyses in a quantitative, objective and informative manner. We also provide empirical evidence of variation of principles within and between both producers and consumers of data analyses. Our work leads to two insights: it suggests a formal mechanism to describe data analyses based on the design principles for data analysis, and it provides a framework to teach students how to build data analyses using formal design principles. Producers may also assign a priori weights to the diﬀerent principles that can guide the construction of an analysis. If a producer’s and consumer’s weights are known to be substantially diﬀerent from each other, then this would be an a priori indication that the analysis may not meet the consumer’s expectations (Figure 6). In such a situation, it may be valuable for the producer and the consumer to come to an agreement over the weighting of the principles before time is spent doing the analysis. Here, the design principles provide a formal articulation of how producer and consumer can agree (or disagree) on the ultimate outcome. The design thinking perspective on data analysis also has useful consequences for teaching data analysis in the classroom, where it is valuable have a formal way to describe what makes data analyses diﬀer from each other and why one type of analysis might be preferable in some circumstances to another type of analysis.

In particular, in teaching about the divergent thinking phase of data analysis, it is common to encourage students to take diﬀerent approaches to addressing a data analytic question. However, we often lack a formal basis for characterizing these diﬀerent approaches for students. The data analytic design principles provide one way to separate diﬀerent approaches and to guide students to explore various approaches to problem solving. Concepts from design thinking can serve as important complements to the traditional notion of statistical thinking. Together, these two forms of thinking provide a more complete road map for developing useful data analyses and present new ways to teach data analyses to novices. The formal speciﬁcation of design principles for data analysis and how they may guide data analysis construction oﬀers a rationale for negotiating qualities of a data analysis between producer and consumer before embarking on substantial data analytic work. An area for possible future work includes measuring to what extent manipulating the weighting of these principles can improve the quality of data analysis.

title: Data Mesh: A Systematic Gray Literature Review
abstract: Data mesh is an emerging domain-driven decentralized data architecture that aims to minimize or avoid operational bottlenecks associated with centralized, monolithic data architectures in enterprises. The topic has piqued the practitioners’ interest, and considerable gray literature exists. At the same time, we observe a lack of academic attempts at defining and building upon the concept. Hence, in this article, we aim to start from the foundations and characterize the data mesh architecture regarding its design principles, architectural components, capabilities, and organizational roles. We systematically collected, analyzed, and synthesized 114 industrial gray literature articles. The resulting review provides insights into practitioners’ perspectives on the four key principles of data mesh: data as a product, domain ownership of data, self-serve data platform, and federated computational governance. Moreover, due to the comparability of data mesh and SOA (service-oriented architecture), we mapped the findings from the gray literature into the reference architectures from the SOA academic literature to create the reference architectures for describing three key dimensions of data mesh: organization of capabilities and roles, development, and runtime. Finally, we discuss open research issues in data mesh, partially based on the findings from the gray literature.

Our main goals were to provide a unified definition of the data mesh concept, create reference architectures for the data mesh, and identify research challenges. We formulated four research questions to achieve these goals: RQ1. What is a data mesh? A data mesh embodies four design principles [ 36 , 39 , 40 ]: data as a product, domain-driven data ownership, self-serve data platform, and federated computational governance. Practitioners may have different perspectives on these principles and experiences applying them. Hence, RQ1 aims to understand and characterize the four principles of data mesh from a practitioner’s standpoint. RQ2. Why is the data mesh needed? Specifically, what are the benefits and concerns of adopting it, and when should it be used? A data mesh has advantages and disadvantages and is not a one-size-fits-all approach for data management.

Data Mesh: A Systematic Gray Literature Review 11:7 3 RQ1: What is Data Mesh? In short, a data mesh is a domain-driven decentralized architecture for managing (analytical) data at scale. It enables the decomposition of an organization’s monolithic analytical data space into data domains aligned with business domains. Such decomposition moves the responsibility of managing and providing high-quality data and valuable insights from the conventional central data team into domain teams that intimately know the data. Dehghani [ 36 , 39 , 40 ] defines the data mesh concept using four principles: (i) data product thinking, (ii) domain ownership of data, (iii) federated computational governance, and (iv) self-serve data platform. Based on the findings from our gray literature, Sections 3.1 to 3.4 aim to study the practitioners’ perspective on these principles and how they expand or implement the principles.

According to literature sources [ 69 , 102 , 123 , 134 , 149 ], a standardized methodology and tools can ensure that all data products define quality on a common set of quality dimensions with shared definitions. A lack of consistent data quality enforcement will lead to data swamps [ 114 , 126 ]. The practitioners propose using a common format for data quality constraints and results [ 162 ] and metadata rules for enforcing the consistent modeling of concepts shared across domains [ 90 ]. Maintaining a Common Business Glossary. Organizations use business glossaries of business terms and their definitions to ensure the same definitions are used throughout the organization when analyzing data. The data mesh principles discourage creating one canonical data model for the whole organization, which goes against decentralization [ 39 ]. However, some gray literature sources recognize the importance of having a shared definition of concepts used throughout the organization (e.g., master and reference data such as customers and currency codes) as this contributes to the interoperability of data products [ 35 , 152 , 156 , 159 ].

In addition, organizations that face many external regulations can use data mesh to ensure compliance as the data mesh facilitates better data governance [ 51 , 107 , 119 ]. Data mesh may not be the most practical data architecture for all organizations. The gray literature mentions several scenarios where the data mesh approach may not be the most suitable option. Lack of Domain-Orientation. The data mesh presumes an organizational structure of independent cross-functional teams aligned with the structures of business domains. If an organization (e.g., typically small and medium-sized companies) does not follow domaindriven design principles and does not have multiple teams who can make data products independently, then the data mesh approach may not fit the organization [ 63 , 70 , 72 , 126 , 135 , 157 ].

The data mesh literature does not explicitly provide an end-to-end methodology for implementing data mesh in or across organizations. However, the literature advocates applying the principles of DDD, product thinking, and platform-based development. In particular, data products should be identified by applying DDD to the data produced by the business domains of the organization [ 1 , 11 , 27 , 32 , 36 , 38 , 40 , 47 , 70 , 86 , 91 , 94 , 102 , 112 , 114 , 121 , 123 , 129 , 133 , 149 , 152 , 155 , 156 , 160 ]. Inspired by a layered model for SOA development [ 115 ], we introduce a layered model for data mesh development that integrates the previously mentioned principles. Figure 7 shows the proposed layered approach to data mesh development. The model comprises seven distinct layers: business domains, data domains, data-bounded contexts, data products, data product components, self-serve platform services, and operating infrastructure.

For example, there may be different categories of customers: online only, physical only, third party, prospect, individual, group, corporation, government, and charity. Managing data for each or subset of these categories might differ, and multiple teams or individuals might be responsible for it. Consequently, multiple bounded contexts emerge within a customer data domain. Various dependencies (design time and runtime) may exist between data bounded contexts. The gray literature recommends using the strategic design patterns of DDD (e.g., customer-supplier and anti-corruption layer) to integrate bounded contexts (i.e., context mapping) [ 156 ]. For example, a bounded context of a composite product can use the anti-corruption layer to minimize the impacts of the changes to the data models of data products from the upstream bounded contexts [ 70 ].

For example, a data product for sales funnel analysis uses the customer search data product to get customers’ browsing history. The funnel analysis product can implement an anti-corruption layer to prevent the adverse effect of changes in browsing history data format. The fourth layer identifies data products within each bounded context. For building applications for a bounded context, DDD recommends applying so-called tactical design patterns: entity, value object, aggregate, service, repositor y, factor y, event, and module. These patterns can be used to enrich a domain model of a bounded context, and the enriched model can be used to derive the application architecture components. For example, in a microservice architecture, services, APIs, and events can be deduced from the domain model using the tactical design patterns [ 147 ]. The

It can be a suitable candidate for a technology-agnostic IaC language that can define the interoperable deployment blueprints for data products and self-serve platform components. Methodologies and Tools for Data Mesh Development and Operation. The data mesh literature [ 40 , 101 , 110 , 111 , 119 , 126 , 129 , 156 ] provides general principles for developing a data mesh architecture, e.g., DDD, product thinking, platform thinking, and computational governance. However, no tools and detailed (empirically validated) methodologies exist for applying these principles to develop and operate a data mesh. Organizations would also need guidance and tools for systematically migrating their legacy data architectures into data mesh while assessing costs and benefits. The research issues may benefit from the rich knowledge about applying DDD for designing and implementing microservices [ 181 ] and migrating legacy monolithic architectures into cloud-based microservices architectures [ 65 ].

Data Product Life Cycle. Data products are at the heart of a data mesh. Each phase of a data product life cycle (e.g., identification, design, development, testing, deployment, discovery, composition, operation, monitoring, and evolution) can have open challenges [ 40 , 42 , 114 , 126 , 129 , 133 , 152 , 155 , 160 ]. For example, the product identification phase decomposes the analytical data landscape of an organization into a set of data products. The partitioning process needs to support applying domain-driven design correctly, ensure the modularity and utility of data products, and consider reuse of the artifacts of the existing data architectures, such as data source systems, data pipelines, machine learning pipelines, documentation, and execution logs. Further exploratory research studies are needed to properly understand the research challenges in each phase of the product life cycle.

Although enterprises are increasingly becoming data-driven, their centralized monolithic data architectures still prevent them from leveraging the full value of their analytical data. The data mesh is an emerging domain-driven decentralized architecture and sociotechnical paradigm that promises to address the limitations of centralized enterprise data architectures. Even though the data mesh is gaining significant attention in the industry, there is an evident scarcity of academic research on the topic. This article systematically selects and reviews 114 industrial gray literature on data mesh to identify key design principles, architectural components, organizational roles, benefits, and concerns. The findings from the review were further enriched with the academic literature from similar domains to create reference architectures for its key dimensions.

title: USSF: A Unified Framework for Screen Standardization in Software Systems
abstract: This paper introduces the Unified Screen Standardization Framework (USSF), a methodological model that consolidates the heterogeneous principles (such as Nielsen’s heuristics, ISO 9241 principles, WCAG accessibility recommendations, Shneiderman’s Eight Golden Rules, Norman’s design principles, etc.) into a coherent, hierarchical structure. USSF employs two novel mechanisms: (1) artifact-based indexing (APP, SCR, DIA, FRM, CMP, WID) to represent application elements in hierarchical form and (2) inheritance with override rules for systematically applying and adapting standards across different levels of user interface elements. The framework enables traceability, scalability and methodological clarity, supporting both usability evaluation and future integration with automated design tools. The USSF could acts as a composite high-level standard that integrates existing standards, principle, heuristics, established usability and accessibility guidelines into a unified model. An illustrative example demonstrates the framework’s applicability, while a discussion highlights its benefits, limitations and potential for empirical validation. The USSF thus provides a novel contribution to human-computer interaction by bridging established guidelines and enabling standardized, traceable and adaptable screen design.

Keywords—unified screen standardization framework, software system, user interface design, screen standardization

Screen standardization in software systems represents a fundamental aspect of UI/UX design. Despite the availability of numerous standards and guidelines, such as Nielsen’s heuristics [1], ISO 9241-110:2020 and its related parts [2], the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) [3], as well as classical principles including Shneiderman’s Eight Golden Rules [4] and Norman’s design principles [5], current literature and practice lack a unified framework that integrates these approaches into a coherent system. This absence gives rise to several critical challenges: • Fragmentation of requirements - different standards and principles are often applied in isolation. • Limited traceability - it is difficult to track how a particular standard is implemented across individual screens or components. • Low comparability - there is no systematic method for comparing different interfaces in terms of compliance with established standards.

Research on screen and user interface standardization has focused on various dimensions: heuristic evaluations, international standards, accessibility guidelines and usability evaluation methodologies. Despite the rich body of work, an integrated approach that unifies these dimensions into a single framework remains absent. Heuristic methods, particularly Nielsen’s heuristics [1], are widely employed for quickly identifying usability problems. While easy to apply, they suffer from subjectivity and limited traceability when applied to large-scale systems. International standards, such as ISO 9241-110:2020 [2], define principles for human-computer interaction and provide a formal framework for ergonomics. However, they often remain too generic and difficult to directly apply to specific interface elements. Similar limitations are observed in ISO 9241-112 and ISO 9241-210, which focus on information structuring and the process of user-centered design [6, 9].

Classical design principles, such as Shneiderman’s Eight Golden Rules [4] and Norman’s principles of design [5], provide strong theoretical foundations for interfac e design. While they play a significant role in both educatio n and practice, they lack a formalized methodology for tr aceability and standardization. In the domain of evaluation methodologies, standards such as ISO 9241-11 [7] and techniques including usability testing, cognitive walkthrough and GOMS (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection rules) [8] provide practical approaches for measurement and analysis. However, these methods ar e primarily focused on the evaluation stage and do not provide mechanisms for integration with the standardization of interface artifacts. Taken together, the existing literature offers a multitude of tools, guidelines and principles, but lacks a meta- model capable of unifying them into a coherent structure.

This gap is precisely what the present study addresses through the proposed Unified Screen Standardization Framework (USSF). The theoretical foundations of the Unified Screen Standardization Framework (USSF) encompass key principles and standards that have shaped the disci pline of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) over several decades. A. Nielsen’s Heuristics Jakob Nielsen’s heuristics, first published in 1994 and subsequently revised [1], consist of ten general principles for the design and evaluation of user interfaces. They are intended as an inspection method, known as heuristic evaluation, where experts assess interfaces against a predefined set of guidelines, identifying usability problems at an early stage. Although these heuristics are informal and inherent ly subjective, they remain one of the most widely used tools for rapid inspection in professional practice and HCI e ducation [10].

B. ISO 9241-110:2020 and Related Parts (112, 125, 210) The ISO 9241 series represents the most influential international standard for the ergonomics of human- system interaction. • ISO 9241-110:2020 defines the Interaction Principles, including task appropriateness, selfdescriptiveness, controllability, conformity with user expectations, error tolerance, suitability for individualization and suitability for learning [2]. • ISO 9241-112:2025 focuses on Principles for the presentation of information, emphasizing perceptual clarity, comprehensibility and consistency of visua l content [9]. • ISO 9241-125:2017 provides guidelines on the visual elements of user interfaces, such as icons, menus and controls [11]. • ISO 9241-210:2019 formulates the principles of human-centred design for interactive systems, integrating HCI approaches into the entire software development lifecycle [6].

Shneiderman emphasized that these rules have univer sal validity because they are grounded in human cogniti ve capabilities. They remain widely applied in both ed ucation and industry as a framework for inspection-based ev aluation [15]. E. Norman’s Principles of Design In his seminal book The Design of Everyday Things (1988, revised in 2013) [5], Donald Norman articula ted a set of principles oriented toward interaction design, with a strong focus on users’ mental models. Unlike Nielsen’s heuristics or Shneiderman’s rules, Norman’s principles are more philosophical and conc eptual. They emphasize that good design should be intuitive , minimizing the need for training or extensive instr uctions [16]. F. Evaluation Methodologies Usability evaluation represents a fundamental stage in software development, providing both objective and subjective data regarding the effectiveness, effici ency and satisfaction of users.

The USSF introduces standardization indexation to ensure traceability and clarity regarding which rules and principles are applied to a given artifact. Each standardization is denoted by its name, while individual principles or rules are accessed through indices. Examples: • Full standardization - only the name is recorded: Nielsen’s Heuristics, WCAG, ISO 9241-110. • Specific principle - an index is added: Nielsen’s Heuristics[5], Norman’s Principles[3]. • Sub-levels - when the standardization includes subprinciples, sub-indices are used: WCAG[2][1]. This scheme follows approaches applied in ontologybased modeling and knowledge traceability systems [21, 22]. The approach is shown in Table II. Standardization Example Notation Interpretation Nielsen’s Heuristics Nielsen’s Heuristics Full set of heuristics Nielsen’s Heuristics (rule) Nielsen’s Heuristics[5] Only heuristic 5 applies WCAG (full) WCAG All WCAG guidelines apply WCAG (sub-rule) WCAG[2][1] WCAG principle 2, guideline 2.1 Norman’s Principles Norman’s Principles[3] Only principle 3 from Norman’s design principles For automated processing, abbreviations of standardizations can be employed: • NH => Nielsen’s Heuristics

• WCAG => Web Content Accessibility Guidelines • SG => Shneiderman’s Golden Rules • ND => Norman’s Design Principles D. Inheritance and Override Mechanism One of the key innovations of the USSF is the introduction of inheritance of standardizations within the artifact hierarchy. By default, each artifact inherits the standards and rules of its parent. When necessary, these can be modified through: • Addition (+) - introducing a new standardization or principle. • Removal (-) - excluding a specific standardization or principle. • Override (no sign) - specifying a new set of standardizations that replaces the inherited ones. Example: APP[0] = Nielsen’s Heuristics, ISO 9241-110 SCR[0][1] = +WCAG, -Nielsen’s Heuristics[3] => This indicates that the screen inherits all standardizations from the application, adds WCAG and removes only Nielsen’s heuristic [3].

CMP[0][1][0] SCR[0][1] +Norman’s Principles[2] Inherited set + Norman principle 2 CMP[0][1][1] SCR[0][1] -ISO 9241-110 All except ISO 9241- E. Traceability Matrix as an Output A fundamental outcome of the USSF methodology is th e generation of a traceability matrix, which systemat ically documents the relationships between interface artif acts and the applied standardizations. By leveraging the ind exing mechanism and the inheritance/override principles, USSF produces a structured representation that ensures b oth consistency and auditability across all interface layers. The traceability matrix fulfills several methodolog ical roles: • Linking artifacts and standards - each APP, SCR, DIA, FRM, CMP or WID is explicitly mapped to the standards and principles inherited or locally applied. • Ensuring hierarchical traceability - the matrix demonstrates how global rules propagate through the hierarchy, while also capturing local exceptions introduced by overrides. • Supporting validation and compliance - the matrix can be used as a formal instrument for verifying

alignment with ISO standards, WCAG compliance and domain-specific usability requirements. • Facilitating knowledge transfer - by presenting an integrated overview, the matrix enables project teams, auditors and stakeholders to understand the applied rules without navigating the full hierarchy. This structured output positions the traceability matrix as a core deliverable of USSF, providing both methodol ogical rigor and practical utility. In large-scale software systems, the matrix also could serves as a foundation for the au tomated generation of compliance reports, CASE tool integration and the creation of dynamic validation dashboards.

This paper introduced the USSF, whose primary aim is to unify and systematize diverse design principles and standardizations. The main contribution of the USSF lies in the introduction of artifact-oriented indexing, combined with a systematic mechanism for inheritance and override of standardization requirements. This approach provides: • Hierarchical traceability - each interface level inherits or modifies the standards of its parent element. • Integration of existing guidelines - the USSF consolidates standards, principles and methodologies into a unified framework. • Scalability - applicable to both small interfaces a nd large, complex applications with multiple artifacts. • Methodological clarity - enables the creation of traceability matrices that link artifacts to specif ic principles and evaluation methods. The USSF can also be interpreted as a composite hig hlevel standard that integrates existing principles and standards into a single structure.

title: Acquiring educational access for neurodiverse learners through multisensory design principles
abstract: Educational interface designers are in an unprecedented position to facilitate autonomous learning in neurodiverse learners (children with special needs). These learners are particularly in need of special design, given the disproportionate impact it can have on their quality of life and the current vulnerability they experience due to changes in special education law. In response to the urgent conditions facing these students, we construct and define a set of design principles that are grounded in maximizing the potential of these learners by importing the meta-cognitive skills, algorithmic structures, and multiple sensory modalities that are both proven successful in their remediation and uniquely suited to technological design adaptation.We draw from our main author's experience as a heavily remediated Dyslexic, a lifelong user of modified, adaptable and assistive technology, and a self-aware learner taught to understand why the methods behind her remediation worked. We additionally draw on our cumulative experience as users, teachers and developers of technology and on interviews with participants from a wide variety of sociocultural functions and pedagogical practices involved with special education. Based upon these and existing methods and applications, we present our insights in the form of guidelines for universal design that have the potential to not only embrace the differences of all learners but to maximize the potential of underserved neurodiverse learners so they can become self-sufficient masters of their own skills and interests across their lifetime.

In this paper we set out to identify design principles for technology that could best help neurodiverse c hildren maximize their potentia l. (We use the term “neurodiverse learners” because the term “special needs” has historically h eld negative connotations and to indicate that these learners are different but not inferior.) Th ere is particular need in this arena because of recent developments in special education law and the outsized benefits these children would receive from such d esign. We draw from the experience of our main author, a dyslexic who experienced technological remediation firsthand and now teaches technology to children herself, who has seen the way technology has evolved -and failed to evolve -to meet new challenges. We believe that these principles, based on our insights into the efficacy of multisensory and multiple modality educational methodologies, will maximize the learning potential of all learners.

Our authors have extensive experience dealing with educational technology and strategies for n eurodiverse learners, particularly dyslexics. The main author of this paper has Dyslexia and ADHD, along with a host of other learning disabilities, and experienced firsthand the failure of traditional classroom methods ( Figure 1). Well into fourth grade, she was still unable to read and incapable of identifying the corresponding sounds to each letter of the alphabet to the point where her tutor said “it was as if she had never seen letters or phonics before — because functionally she had not.” All remediation failed until she began multisensory programs, provided under the auspices of Massachusetts special education Law ( Table 1). Aware of the role that both law and technology played in her own successful remediation, she became interested in how advances in technology could supplement a special education law that had been vastly weakened since her own experiences. One coauthor on this paper is also an attorney who has been a part of the dyslexic’s ecosystem as a family support member and has experience with the legal aspects of disability. The third author is a media designer who has worked closely engaging in participatory design with sight -and hearing- impaired people for over a decade. Because diagnosing and dealing with their needs is time -consuming, they have less time for social interaction, causing t hem to lose the opportunity to learn social cues and customs that will benefit them going forward. They are further impacted by the need to travel to a special needs class or get special attention within the mainstream class, which singles them out in front of their peers. Because technology has become so normalized, peers will not consider students strange if they have an iPad or mobile phone, removing one barrier to positive social interaction. Any help in remediation that doesn’t stigmatize the student must be considered desirable, if not essential, to the student’s mental health and their ability to dedicate themselves to their important work. 2.2.4 Self-sufficiency beyond the classroom The private nature of a student’s interaction with mobile devices and ap plications allows the student freedom to experiment as to what methods work for him or her without concern for the social stigmas outlined above.

Our approach to developing multisensory technology recognizes that there is much to be gained by a universal design for learning (UDL) approach [1]. A multisensory universal design learning approach that works well for neurodiverse learners can also benefit mainstream learners [11]. For these traditional learners, incorporating multisensory aspects can expand the appeal and efficacy of these programs as well as benefit those who happen to be tuned to different types of intelligences [6]. However, the mere presence of multisensory stimulation within an app by itself does not guarantee its educational benefit. OG and VV work because they help communicate core learning concepts through different modalities. The use of multisensory representation is designed to convey redundant and complementary representations of concepts that can broaden the student’s experience of that concept.

In some cases, cute animations are given as rewards for correct answers. In other instances, arbitrary restrictions are imposed on the user’s multisensory interactions (e.g. when tracing letters, requiring that the fingers approach and follow the line in a particular direction to create the letter). Some informal quotes from users we interviewed on these other programs give an idea of the pros and cons of existing multisensor y technology: “He likes to start the letter ‘O’ from the bottom, but the program forces him to start his ‘O’ from the top.” – Parent It’s easier to pay more attention when it’s a viewframe with touching because it’s part of a story. Better than copying down notes, just copying down and forgetting the next day. – 4 th grader “There are three choices, and he’s memorized the right one, but I am not sure if he really recognizes the letters because they always appear in the same place.”-‐-‐Parent

The first principle we propose is that educational technology should contain fixed content but fluid access. Apps or tech that allow children to reach the correct answers in only one way are no better than classroom methods that ignore modality strengths and the advantages of multisensory teaching. We therefore propose the idea of fluid access, meaning that multiple modalities should be available to get students to one unchanging truth or rule. For example, a counting app that gives children an opportunity to learn through multiple modalities might show an image of the appropriate number of objects, speak the number aloud, and/or buzz the equivalent number of times in their hands. By keeping the method of accessing the answer fluid, the app ensures that children can learn whether through multisensory application or through a modality in which they have a particular strength.

We believe these principles will benefit designers as well as learners. Fixed content provides clear guideposts for them to follow, while the feedback practice provides ample data for quality assurance. Universal design practices also ensure that designers are pitching their products at the largest possible market to users who will rea p the maximum possible benefits. While the best outlet at the moment is for mobile technology, designers can apply these principles to emerging technologies as well . It is imperative that designers remain cognizant of the unique position they are in. At th is point in the intersection of special education law and technology, designers have the ability to do justice that has normally been the purview of the law. Though this paper addresses only American law, its lessons emphasize why the legal framework for a ccess should be kept in mind no matter what country is the primary audience for design.

If properly designed, ed tech can not only teach these children content areas like math or reading but the unique ways in which their brains work, helping them form learning strategies that will see them through the rest of their lives. By this simple truth, designers can ensure that even as neurodiverse learners’ disabilities survive the classroom, so will their autonomy.

title: Introduction to Initial HCI Engineering Design Principles for Domestic Energy Planning and Control
abstract: This chapter introduces HCI-EDPs for the application domain of domestic energy planning and control. The introduction comprises: a conception of declarative EDPs; an 'instance-first' strategy for developing such principles, and a conception of human-computer systems, required for such principles. The chapter constitutes the basis for the following chapter on the development of initial HCI-EDPs to support the more effective design of interactive domestic energy planning and control systems.

The development of HCI-EDPs is one response to the challenge of increasing the reliability of HCI design knowledge to support design practice more effectively. The case study makes progress towards such HCI-EDPs in the application domain of domestic energy planning and control. The progress constitutes potential carry forward for future HCI-EDP research.

The partial design problem and solution operationalisations are the instantiations of a general design pr oblem and its general design solution, as shown in Figure 2.3. The specific design problem and solution operationalisations represent the scoping of an HCI discipline as engineering. The partial design problem and solution operationalisations represent the application of HCI engineering design knowledge. They are “partial” because they solve only part of the specific design problem.

This case study restricts itself to declarative rather than to procedural HCI-EDPs. Procedural principles prescribe the methods for solving a general design problem

optimally. Declarative principles prescribe the features and properties of artefacts, or systems that constitute an optimal solution to a general design problem. Three types of HCI-EDPs are identified: 1. Decomposition knowledge (Kde) is conceptualised as the means of instantiating a partial design problem from a specific design problem. Kde requires declarative knowledge of the general design problem of which the partial design problem is the instance (see Figure 2.3). 2. The specific design problem and solution may not be required for HCI engineering design practice. It may be possible to instantiate a partial design problem from the user or any other requirements using Kde. It may also be possible to instantiate part of the artefact specification using Kre. However, it is expected that the specific design problem and solution are required, at least, as the object of further research. The declarative knowledge required for Kde, Kso, and Kre is a general design problem and its general design solution, conceptualised by a gener al desired performance and a general actual performance, respectively. A general design problem and its general design solution are general over types of user, types of computer, and types of domain of application. Desired performance and actual performance are conceptualised further below, following Dowell and Long ( 1989).

Assessment of the strategy comprises: acquisition (or not) of initial HCI-EDPs; assessment of the status of such acquired principles; and discussion of the strategy and conceptions, following the acquisition (or not) of initial HCI-EDPs. A conception here is a set of concepts and their relations, which are abstractions over a class of objects, based on their common aspects. Conceptualisation is the process of generating a conception. Operationalisation is the process of instancing a conception to produce an operationalisation. An operationalisation of a conception is a set of less abstract concepts (related to the concepts in the conception) that ultimately reference observables in the world. Dowell and Long (1989) claim that, for the acquisition of the knowledge to support HCI- EDPs, the operationalisation of the specific design problems and solutions needs to be explicit and formal.

The case study is restricted to the acquisition of cognitive HCI-EDPs. That is, excluding conative or affective principles. Cognitive processes and representations are relatively well defined , compared to the others. The latter constitute objects for possible future research. However, reference also needs to be made to: additional concepts, current solutions, and “best-practice.” As concerns “additional concepts” to operationalise specific design problems and solutions, these are derived from a conception of human-computer systems costs. Human-computer costs are poorly conceptualised by specific design problems and solutions (for example, relative to task quality). Section 2.3 proposes such a conception. As concerns “current solutions,” it is easier to operationalise existing, installed, specific design solutions than to operationalise specific design problems.

Also, that a specific design solution exists. “Best practice” for developing design solutions is considered to be the best design practice at the time of HCI-EDP acquisition. At the time of the present case study, the latter was considered to include the application of a structured analysis and design method (MUSE - Method for USability Engineering; Lim and Long, 1994), the use of design guidelines and evaluations. However, there was no consensus, concerning HCI best practice at the time and so alternative design knowledge and practices could have been applied. Likewise , today’s best practice would be expected to inc lude design knowledge and practices, developed since the time of the case study. Such design knowledge and practices would be expected to include among others those propagated by Ritter et al. (2014), Hartson and Pyla (2018), Kim (2020), and Zagalo (2020).

The strategy for developing HCI engineering principles is characterised as “bottom-up” and cautious, or even sceptical ( Stork, 1999). The cautious approach entails either that steady progress is made towards HCI-EDPs or that the research direction is abandoned. The cautious approach also accepts that HCI-E DPs may not be acquired initially. An alternative “top-down” strategy would be to postulate operationalisable and testable HCI-EDPs, based on their conceptualisation. Such principles could then be operationalised and tested. The strategy is considered bold, given the current modest understanding of HCI-EDPs. The likelihood of identifying such a principle might be low. However, the effort for each attempt would be less than with the bottom-up strategy. The top-down strategy is rejected here. The low likelihood of identifying an HCI-EDP is insufficient to merit the effort of each attempt.

The cycle operationalisations identify the concepts operationalised to support informal checking; 3. such principles be generalised. The gener alisation here is over the two development cycles; and 4. such principles be tested. The testing here is the informal evaluation of the two development cycles.

The research strategy is to develop HCI knowledge for HCI practice in the longer term, as HCI- EDPs. Shorter-term research benefits may also accrue. For example, a medium-term research (and practice) benefit is a version of MUSE ( Lim and Long, 1994 ) that supports a more complete, coherent, and consistent specification of the design problem and solution.

Practice Scenario 2.1: Applying Conceptions for HCI Engineering Design Principles to an Additional Domain of Application Select a domain of application, with which you are familiar or which is of interest to you or preferably both. The domain should be other than that of domestic energy planning and control. • Apply the conceptions for the domestic energy planning and control (see § 2.1 ) to the novel domain of application. title: Personalising learning: towards a coherent learning design framework
abstract: The vision of a Personalised Learning (PL) experience in education is a long-standing notion advocated by educators. Research literature accounts for several pedagogical and technological approaches to tailor learning to learners' variability. This paper aims to contribute to PL and Learning Design (LD) research by conceptualising CPELDS (Coherent PErsonalised Learning DeSign) as a framework outlining consistent PL design principles. CPELDS blends learner profiles addressing the dimensions of interests, strengths and needs with personalisation principles. Considering evidence about the effectiveness of Universal Design for Learning in empirical studies in special education, we transform and augment its guidelines into personalisation principles of CPELDS to address broader learners' variability. The personalisation principles employed involve (i) fostering learner's engagement, (ii) providing alternative information perception and comprehension modes, including differentiation, and (iii) supporting alternative means for learners' action and expression to demonstrate acquired knowledge and skills. We anticipate the conceptualisation of CPELDS to stimulate the representational form of an LD tool towards supporting educators as designers of PL.
subdocument:
In this line of research, deploying technology-driven personalisation has been extensively addressed in Adaptive Systems. On the other hand, [3] claimed that PL focuses on the learner’s motivation, engagement, and voice rather than technology driving learning. This diversity as well as plurality of pedagogical and technological approaches to personalisation, usually confuses educators in terms of what means to employ and how to tailor learning to learners’ variability in their everyday practice. Indeed, research on different PL design principles and the effectiveness of their implementations is limited, with very little research reporting PL in “real-world” education settings [4]. A main contribution to this line of research may emerge by considering the importance of educators being able to design learning experiences [5] and prioritising their role as designers for PL.

This paper provides such a contribution to the research field of PL by conceptualising the CPELDS (Coherent PErsonalised Learning DeSign) as a framework blending dimensions of learner profile with personalisation principles toward employing consistent PL design principles. Furthermore, supporting educators as PL designers aligns with LD orientation to develop LD tools that accommodate their design practices [6]. However, existing LD tools’ approaches are inconclusive in the level of guidance and support provided to designers [7]. On the one hand, research teams acknowledged the need to support educators in applying effective pedagogy and/or using technology. Indicative examples of such approaches are the Learning Designer [8] integrating the Conversational Framework in the articulation of learning activities’ pedagogy , the WebCollage [9] integrating collaborative patterns for the organisation of collaborative learning techniques, and the PeerLAND integrating TPACK framework for the design and evaluation of learning designs [10].

On the other hand, researchers argued in favour of LD tools not embedding any specific teaching/learning scaffold to support transferability across different contexts of use, disciplines, target populations, etc [6]. Focusing on supporting personalisation in LD tools, we noted that it had been mainly addressed at deploying learning designs without being attentive to scaffolding the design process per se. Indicative examples of such approaches are the DEPIT- App enabling different difficulty levels in learning activities [11], the WISE enabling the provision of alternative educational resources [12], and LAMS enabling the realization of alternative learning pathways [13]. Asserting that the diversity of approaches to personalisation challenges research ers to employ consistent design features in LD tools, we anticipate CPELDS’ added value to include researchers’ quest to develop LD tools supporting educators to design PL interventions.Our research team’s future research agenda includes developing and evaluating an LD tool deploying CPELDS.

We conceptualised CPELDS by blending dimensions of learner profile and personalisation principles, as presented in Fig 1. In what follows, we elaborate on its elements. A. Learner Profile Reviewing principles of PL interventions, we noticed that research is deluged with learner profiling as an essential principle of PL [2], [4]. However, the plethora of learner profile dimensions considered made deciding which to include in CPELDS quite challenging. Influe nced by an extensive study conducted on behalf of the Gates Foundation regarding the implementation of PL in 62 American schools [14], we concluded in the following most influential profile dimensions: x Interests refer to addressing and stimulating learner interests, either personal or content-specific. x Strengths refer to accommodating learner strengths, e.g., personal traits or academic performance. x Needs refer to catering to learner needs, e.g., needs for perceiving and comprehending information, degree of support, and learning difficulties.

Thus, CPELDS blends a pedagogical perspective underpinned by interest-based learning, strengths-based learning, and differentiated learning with affordances of teachers ’ everyday practice. B. Personalisation Principles Universal Design for Learning (UDL), a well-accepted framework for designing learning interventions in special education [15], caught our attention. We acknowledge that in its scope to provide effective learning for all learners, UDL may serve as a starting point to develop a unifying framework that could foundationally build PL across research, practice, and policy [16]. Based on the UDL framework, we transform and augment its guidelines by reconsidering, redefining and recontextualising them into personalisation principles. We employ the following personalisation principles: i) Engagement involves fostering learners’ engagement during the learning process with several means.

CPELDS adopts the three-fold approach of UDL guidelines: x recruiting interest, e.g. by providing learners with opportunities for individual choice and autonomy and/or optimising content relevance, value and authenticity; x sustaining effort and persistence, e.g. by giving feedback and/or enhancing the communication between learner and teacher and/or peers; and x self-regulation, e.g. by promoting self-evaluation and reflection. ii) Information involves providing alternative information perception and comprehension modes, including differentiation. Specifically, the personalisation principle of Information in CPELDS broadens UDL’s Representation perspective to include con tent and process differentiation practices. iii) Action and expression refer to encouraging learners express their comprehension of learning content based on their interests and demonstrate knowledge and skills by leveraging their strengths.

CPELDS incorporates learner choice to blend dimensions of learner profile and personalisation principles. Recent research on PL interventions involves employing learner choice [17] instead of providing learners with customised learning paths, contents, scaffolds, and/or assessment reports [16]. CPELDS calls educators’ attention to providing alternative options for realising PL activities to actualise learner choice. These options involve applying appropriate resources, technologies and assessments to accommodate learners’ profiles so that learners choose the option that best fits their profile. For example, a learning activity blending the dimension interests of learner profile with the personalisation principle of engagement may address a learner ’s interest in sports by recruiting interest for a favourite sport. This approach may include providing alternative options for an assignment’s content, thus optimising co ntent relevance, value and authenticity.

A learning activity blending the dimension needs of learner profile with the personalisation principle of information may blend the need for information perception and comprehension either dynamically or statically with alternative options for providing educational material (e.g., video or text). And a learning activity blending the dimension strengths of learner profile with the personalisation principle of action and expression may blend the strength of digital skills with alternative options for information perception and comprehension (e.g., producing an artefact digitally or nondigitally).

Our future research agenda includes developing an LD tool deploying CPELDS. Due to space limitations in the current paper, we briefly elaborate on (i) the representational form of learning activities in such a tool and (ii) the scaffolding mechanisms for applying CPELDS. The representational form of a learning activity should incorporate a dedicated section for describing PL. Such a section should be controlled by a switch indicating whether PL is applied in the specific activity to activate/deactivate the fields included. Regarding the fields needed, they should include representing all the elements of CPELDS, i.e., dimensions of the learner profile and personalisation principles. These fields’ representational forms could be either drop-down menus or checkboxes, or even text fields. Following a participatory design approach, our research team will explore these forms in forthcoming studies to consider practitioners’ feedback.

Regarding how an LD tool may support a designer, features that havebeen highly appreciated in LD tools’ evaluation studies include providing onlin e help on a learning design’s representation and some kind of “conceptual help” in the LD process [17]. In this line, a basic scaffolding mechanism may involve descriptions of CPELDS’ elements and exemplar learning activities. A state -of-the-art mechanism providing “conceptual help” may involve a Recommender System (RS) integrated into the LD tool. Such an approach may include the well-established RSs practice in repositories following a macro recommendation of learning designs developed in the LD tool. Furthermore, it is worth considering the perspective of LD tools providing a micro recommendation form that supports the LD process by recommending specific elements within a learning design [18].
